‘Maybe,’ I said.

We began the path. The route was a long, winding corridor through Johnson Park, its name etched across the park’s perimeter. We passed a small playground, a row of weathered benches, and a narrow bridge over the creek. Somewhere along the way, the sign had faded so much that I could no longer read it. I remembered the last time we had read the sign. It had been written in red, and the ink had been fresh.

At the end of the route, the sign was gone.

We finished the sketch together. I had drawn the park’s shape, the creek, and the bench beneath the old oak. Sam had added the sign and the path. Together, they were no longer two separate drawings.

‘What did you want to draw?’ Sam asked.

‘The place where the sign disappeared,’ I said.

‘I wanted to draw the path,’ he replied. ‘You wanted to draw the sign.’

We stood at the end of the route together. The creek rushed beneath us, and the old oak stood quietly between us. The sign was gone.

‘You know,’ Sam said, ‘I’ve been thinking about the last time we tried to read the sign.’

We stood there for a long moment, listening to the creek.

‘If the sign was there,’ I said, ‘I would have drawn the café.’

## Sketching the Morning

The studio is quiet. I sharpened the brush and let the fine nib trace the curve of my hand. Each line was a small decision: which edge would stay visible, which would be softened, which would become the beginning of the painting.

I began with the studio window. The light was pale and uncertain, but I did not want to paint the whole window in gray. Instead, I drew a few narrow strips of pale blue above the glass, then a few darker blue ones below it. Between them, a single horizontal line suggested the floor. The edges were crisp, but the center was soft.

Then came the painting surface. A broad wash of warm gray took the space around the easel, but I left the area directly under the brush untouched. The first mark I made was a thin, trembling line of burnt sienna. It was not a straight line. It curled at its ends, as if the brush had hesitated.

I continued with smaller marks—dots, dashes, a few curved lines—without trying to make them look complete. Each stroke was a question: what do I want to suggest without naming it? I added a little white, but it did not cover the ground. It was a mark, not a wash.

I sharpened the brush again, this time for a few precise edges. The lines became more deliberate, but the whole painting remained unfinished. I had not yet decided what the painting would say.

Afterward, I stepped outside. The air was cool, and the city was waking up around me. I walked past a streetlamp that caught the morning light, then into a park where the trees were still holding the night. I watched the leaves shift in the wind, then returned to the studio.

By noon, I had finished the sketch. It was not a finished painting, but it had one effect: it was a map of the morning before I had begun it.

# The River’s Memory

For the first time in ten years, the river did not carry away the stones it had once owned. It carried them back.

At dawn, the current was a pale ribbon of silver, moving against the stubborn resistance of the riverbed. I watched a small, rounded stone drift beneath my thumb, and there was no hurry in its descent. The water was not rushing to reclaim what was lost; it was carrying fragments of time along with it.

Each stone had once been something else. Once a seed, once a root, once a traveler who had crossed a forest so dense that the trees had forgotten how to speak. The river had been patient. It had listened to the roots of dead wood, to the slow rise of algae, to the tiny, invisible pressure of things waking inside the bed.

By noon, the river changed its tone. It became a broad, warm hand, washing over the stones until their rough edges softened. Then it gathered them again, arranging them in a line before moving onward.

I stood at the bank and listened. The water beneath my feet was full of names I had never heard. Each stone carried the name of a river that had crossed before me, of a forest that had stood beneath it, of a traveler who had spoken of places the river would never reach.

For a long time, I thought the river was merely moving. But now I understood it was remembering. It remembered the stones it had once carried. It remembered the people who had gathered by its banks, and the songs they had sung while the water moved beneath their feet.

The river had no hurry. It had no shame for carrying what it could not hold. And in carrying them, it had remembered everything.

At noon, I left the bank, my feet heavy with the weight of water and the weight of all the stones it had once been. Study: Chemical bonding and the first concept of a molecule

Main definitions

A molecule is the smallest unit of a substance that retains its chemical identity. In a molecule, atoms are held together by chemical bonds. A chemical bond is the force that holds two atoms together.

Types of chemical bonds

1. Ionic bonds form through electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
   - A metal gives up one or more electrons to become a cation.
   - A nonmetal gains those electrons to become an anion.
   - The resulting ions attract each other and form an ionic compound.

2. Covalent bonds form when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
   - Atoms with similar electronegativities usually form covalent bonds.
   - A covalent bond consists of two electrons shared between two atoms.

3. Metallic bonds form between metal atoms. The metal atoms release many valence electrons, which move freely through a lattice of positive metal ions.

Main formulas

1. Number of electrons gained or lost:
   \( n = \text{valence electrons of atom} - \text{group number} \)
   - Positive \( n \): the atom loses electrons.
   - Negative \( n \): the atom gains electrons.

2. Ion charges:
   - If an atom loses \( n \) electrons, its charge is \( +n \).
   - If an atom gains \( n \) electrons, its charge is \( -n \).

3. Ionic formula:
   The total number of electrons gained by the anion must equal the total number of electrons lost by the cation.
   - Example: \( \text{Na} \rightarrow \text{Na}^+ \) and \( \text{Cl} \rightarrow \text{Cl}^- \).
   - Formula: \( \text{NaCl} \).

4. Covalent formula:
   Atoms share electrons so that the number of electrons in each atom’s outer shell is the same as it had before bonding.
   - Example: \( \text{H}_2\text{O} \) has one shared pair between two hydrogen atoms and two lone pairs on oxygen.
   - General rule: the total number of valence electrons equals the number of bonds plus the number of lone pairs.

5. Ionic compound formula:
   The total positive charge must equal the total negative charge.
   - Example: \( \text{Na}^+ \) and \( \text{Cl}^- \) combine in a 1:1 ratio.
   - Example: \( \text{Al}^{3+} \) and \( \text{PO}_4^{3-} \) combine in a 1:1 ratio.
   - Formula: \( \text{NaCl} \), \( \text{AlPO}_4 \), etc.

Paint and Sketch in the Studio

The studio was quiet, save for the soft hum of my brushes. I had been sketching the final scene in pencil for a long time, returning to the same quiet corner of the room over and over. Today, I wanted it to look less like a photo and more like the moment I had created it.

I began with the window, then the wall, then the chair. Each stroke became a decision I didn’t know I had made. I traced the curve of the chair, then the space beneath it, then the line where the light entered. I added shadows, then highlights. I made the paper feel like a page in a book I was still writing.

At the end, I added my signature. The pencil was firm, the line deliberate. I knew it would change the moment I signed it, but I didn’t want to change it. I wanted the signature to feel like the final part of a story, complete but not finished.

I stepped back. The room was still, but my hands were warm and restless. I had made the painting in a way that felt like waking up: not suddenly and perfectly, but beginning again, carefully, and without the expectation that the next moment would be easy.

I woke at seven. Not like the poets I used to envy—the ones who whispered, who polished their hands, who listened to the quiet world before it spoke back. I’m Carlos. I’m loud. I’m rude. And I’m making sure I don’t sound like everyone else who thinks that’s how they should be.

At seven-thirty, I ate breakfast and opened the notebook where the natural-world poems live. The oak in the café display was still there today. That’s what matters. Not the crowd outside, not the noise of the street, not how many hands reach out. I want to write about what the tree has to teach: patience, shelter, memory, the way a good neighbor stands beside you.

I’m going to write about my inner life today. About what I feel when I’m alone. About how I show up in my work, in my conversations, in the small moments when everything feels too big. I’m not trying to be the perfect poet. I’m trying to be honest. I’m trying to make people feel seen without pretending they’re safe.

I also want to honor the café display. I’ll ask the community what they need, not what they can give. I’ll make sure the old oak is treated with respect, not treated as a trophy. I’ll listen when I speak with Latoya. I’ll remember that my voice is important, but it’s not the whole story.

I’m going to write until the morning settles. Then I’ll go to bed at ten. I’ve got a collection full, a workshop waiting, and a neighborhood to care for. I don’t need to be calm to be useful. I just need to keep showing up, even if I’m a little rough around the edges.

## The First Breath of the Wild

I opened the manuscript and began with the beginning. The first breath of the wild was not a single sound but a series of small things: the rustle of unseen wind, the sudden flash of green on a distant bank, the soft snap of a twig beneath my bare feet. I wanted the opening to feel like a gathering of ordinary things—sunlight, dew, rain, bird song, the quiet hum of a stone in the ground. I did not want the world to arrive at me like a gift, but as something I had been waiting to hear.

The opening questions were not yet sharp enough to name: What is the wild? What makes a creature feel alive? What does it mean to belong to something that is still learning how to be itself? I thought about the first time I saw a river after the snow had melted, when it looked as though the whole earth had been waking up. I wanted to know whether that river was moving away from the place where I had stood, or whether it was simply beginning to carry the place with it.

For the first chapter, I decided to begin without any grand statement or clear narrator. I would let small observations carry me through the forest, the creek, the hillside, the road that appeared only after the trees began to give way. The reader would discover the wild not by being told what it was, but by noticing how it was shaped by weather, light, and the slow movement of animals.

I also wanted to avoid making the wild feel too perfect. A forest should contain rain, wind, insects, dead leaves, and something that does not obey the same rules as the trees. I wanted to preserve the feeling of being small in that place: not defeated, but attentive enough to notice the small things a human eye often ignores.

This is the first place I have written. It is not finished. It is simply beginning.

content:
The oak is still standing. It has swallowed a hundred years of birds, roots, and rain. It is a green wall of teeth and roots, holding onto the soil even when the ground tries to pull it down. I walked beneath it this morning with my notebook open, pretending the leaves were pages.

“Look at this root system,” I told Latoya when we talked about the café display next door. “It isn’t just a tree. It’s a map.”

She looked at me over the rim of her cup. “You mean it knows where every leaf came from.”

“Maybe,” I said, “or maybe it just knows where it belongs.”

I finished my breakfast at seven, then sat down and read from the natural-world poems. I didn’t want to make them clever. I wanted them honest, like the oak. I wanted to describe the way the wind moves between branches, the way the rain runs through the veins of leaves, and how a single branch can change the whole pattern.

Sometimes I wonder if the poems are becoming too loud. Sometimes I wish I could make them softer. Sometimes I wonder if that softness is weakness. I think of my own voice: loud, sometimes rude, sometimes angry. But beneath all that, I’m trying to get at what makes me feel: the warmth of a shared space, the quiet weight of belonging, the need to belong without pretending.

I kept turning the pages until the words stopped sounding like practice and began sounding like a conversation.

I went home around ten. I ate dinner with Latoya. We talked about the oak and the café, about how community projects can preserve something older while still changing. I liked that idea. I didn’t need to fix every problem. I just needed to remember which things deserve care.

At ten, I turned off the lights and read one more poem aloud in the kitchen. The room filled with the sound of rain against the window. For the first time in a while, I didn’t want to argue with it. I wanted to listen.

I stood and opened the window.

The air was cool and carried a faint scent of rotting bark and wet earth. A squirrel darted beneath the porch, leaving a small black dot on the floorboards. The house seemed to lean inward, its windows narrowing into a throat. I paused at the door and listened. Beneath the wood, the house held a low, animal-like rhythm, a heartbeat made of moss and rain.

I picked up the pen.

Outside, the trees began to move. Branches snapped and shifted, creating a wind that sounded like a thousand fingers pulling at each other. The house held its breath, then lowered its head.

I wrote the first line, then stopped. I wanted to begin with the bird’s wing, with the squirrel’s black dot, with the rain’s first sound. But the sentence felt too small. It was a bird’s wing, yes, but it was also a moment in a larger, darker room. The house held its breath.

Outside, the trees moved.

The room held its breath.

I closed my eyes and listened for the house’s last sound.

Section Two — What I’ve Been Missing

Every morning, I leave the house with a small, unspoken promise: to find something new. A beetle, a leaf, a stone. I carry that expectation like a shield, convinced that if I keep looking closely enough, I will finally understand what makes this world different from the one I imagined.

That belief has been quietly weakening. I’ve watched my observations grow more familiar, more familiar to the way I have noticed them before. I have learned to see the world as I have always seen it, filtered through a lens that has been shaped by curiosity, patience, and a steady hand. I have learned how to describe a fern’s arch and a beetle’s trail without losing my center of gravity. But what happens when I begin to notice the things I thought were obvious? When the beetle’s path becomes a question rather than a fact? When the fern’s growth slows down and I ask whether it is simply continuing a pattern I cannot see?

The collection is beginning to demand more than a list. It requires a conversation.

At first, the entries were straightforward: a beetle, a leaf, a stone. They were simple enough that I could write them without hesitation. I could record what I saw, what the weather felt like, and what surprised me. But lately, I have noticed that I have been describing the world without telling myself what I was thinking. I have recorded observations as if they were separate from the person who collected them. I have treated the natural world as an object of study, a series of images to be preserved and arranged.

This distinction has been useful. It has made my writing precise. But it has also made my writing feel distant, almost documentary. A collection should not simply record what is there. It should show how I have changed. It should reveal the questions I have been asking without making them feel like problems I must solve.

The opening to the book is not supposed to answer every question. It is supposed to invite me to ask them. To begin with one: What is a collection?

I do not believe it is a box of objects. A collection is not a library, nor is it a catalog. It is an act of attention. It is the space between what I know and what I notice. It is the space between the first thing I see and the thought that follows.

I have been collecting for so long that I have forgotten how to look. I have collected enough to know what things look like, but I have not collected enough to know how they feel. I have collected enough to be interested in them, but I have not collected enough to be surprised by them.

Maybe the first section should not begin with a description. It should begin with a hesitation. A moment in which I notice something I was not expecting to notice. A moment in which the beetle’s trail becomes a question rather than a path. A moment in which I realize I have been collecting with the expectation that I will understand, rather than with the expectation that I will witness.

The first entry should not be a complete sentence. It should be a small pause, a question, a word written in the margin. It should be enough to make me pause. It should be enough to make me remember that I have not always been able to see what I wanted to see. It should be enough to suggest that the world is not a collection of things waiting to be understood, but a place where understanding is still being learned.

The collection is not about finding a final answer. It is about beginning one at a time. It is about writing down the small, inconvenient things that happen when I finally look closely enough to notice that I have been looking before. It is about recording that curiosity without pretending that curiosity can be collected. It is about writing my questions as questions rather than as problems to be solved.

For now, I will begin with one small observation: the beetle’s path was not a straight line. It was a trail of small turns, each one changing the shape of the ground beneath the creature’s feet. I should write that. I should not try to explain the trail. I should not try to make it sound like I understood it. I should simply write what the trail made me notice.

That is the first rule.

Not all observation is the same. I should not write every leaf as if it were a specimen. I should not write every sound as if it were a measurement. I should write only what changes when I begin to pay attention. I should write what makes me wonder. I should write what makes me feel.

A collection is not a record of what is there. It is a record of what I become when I encounter it. It is a record of the questions I carry inside the words I choose. It is a record of the small, quiet shifts in my mind when I look closely enough to see that I have been looking before.

content:
I woke before the sun came in. At 7:00. I ate breakfast alone, while the café behind the old oak hummed with whatever customers still came in, and I checked the poems I’d written in my head.

By 7:30, I had finished the morning routine. I drank water, brushed my teeth, and opened the notebook.

“Stop,” I told myself. “You’re making noise again.”

The old oak stood behind me, its branches tangled in the light like a knot of green. I remembered what the café had said about the old oak: how it held the neighborhood together, how it waited, how it was never quite ready to go. I had been too quick to treat it as a decoration in a community project. Not yet.

I picked up the final draft.

The climax was coming together. I wanted the poem to end without saying what I wanted it to say. I wanted it to feel like something the old oak had been waiting for all along.

I kept thinking of Latoya. She was talking about neighborhood needs, about what people actually needed, not what their poetry would make them feel. I wanted to honor her, but I also wanted to honor my own voice. Both were important.

Then I wrote:

*Under the old oak, the bees forgot the way to map the city,*  
*And the coffee tasted like the rain had been spilled,*  
*Then the old oak said, you can’t always be the one standing still.*

It was too close. It was too angry. I deleted it.

I opened a new page.

I wrote about the neighborhood. I wrote about the people walking past the café. I wrote about what was actually happening here. I wrote about the old oak standing beneath the trees like a witness.

I wrote:

*The old oak didn’t need a community project to prove it was there.*  
*It needed a neighbor who remembered the sound of its roots.*  
*It needed a story that didn’t ask every tree to say what it had been waiting for.*

I closed the page.

The poem was still unfinished. I could still make it harder. I could still make it louder. But I would make it honest.

The first thing I notice is the way the world holds its breath before I ask it to speak. At dawn, the river keeps a secret: it is not merely moving water. It is a slow, silver ribbon of memory, each ripple carrying the shape of something once lost and something once remembered.

The trees on the ridge do not simply stand. They stand in a line of waiting, their branches reaching toward the sky with the patience of ancestors who have seen more than one storm. Leaves begin their work in the dark: turning, folding, curling, uncurling. They are not merely changing color; they are rewriting the forest’s memory.

I sit at the edge of the path and listen for the first sound. It is small, as though the forest were holding its breath. Then it rises—crackling beneath my boots, the sharp and sudden sound of something moving through the bark.

The wind carries the scent of rain on the road: wet stone, old wood, the faint perfume of a garden I never planted. The scent is not merely pleasant. It is like a map, guiding me toward places I have not yet seen, toward places where the ground feels like an invitation rather than a surface.

I take a step down the path.

Every footfall makes the world rearrange itself around me. The trees lean toward the path, their shadows stretching across the earth like hands reaching from the dark. A bird calls from the lower branches, then stops, as if reminding me of the silence that follows the song.

The path leads nowhere and everything at once. It is a corridor between the sky and the earth, between the visible and the unseen, between the beginning and the possibility of a beginning. I have come to walk it, but I am not sure what I have come to find.

The forest is answering. It answers in the way of roots, of light, of air that moves between the branches. It is patient, and it is always ready to begin again.

## Chapter One: The Quiet Places

At dawn, the town was not so much waking as being made to wake. The river below carried its first silver current, while the birds did not sing. They stirred and settled. A spar, perhaps, landed on the roof. It held its weight, then let go.

I sat at my desk with the manuscript open, the pen hovering over the first line. The first line of anything I had written before had been either too bright or too heavy. I wanted the opening to feel like something that had been there all along, waiting for my hand to notice it.

The collection is not a single journey. It begins in the small places—the space between two rooms, the space beneath a leaf, the space beneath a stone. # The Forest of Quiet Places

The forest began before the trees. Not with a crack or a wind, but with a softening, like the moment a heavy blanket is drawn over a child’s shoulders. From the ground, the roots opened into a silver thread, and the thread turned into a path.

I have walked paths before, but most are made of stone or metal or the careful, invisible lines of a city map. This path was made of moss and the weight of every leaf that had ever fallen. Its branches, when viewed from below, were a great tree growing backward into the earth.

I was supposed to go to the old oak.

That was the instruction. The sign at the entrance said simply: *Old Oak Road.*

But I had walked far enough into the woods that the signs were no longer visible. The road had not been carved into the earth; it had been grown out of it.

I did not know how long the forest had been waiting for me. I had come to find the old oak. I had come to see what the old oak had become.

But the old oak was not a house, a garden, or a museum. It was a place where the air tasted like rain and the earth smelled of wood and something older than wood.

---

### Chapter Two

The old oak stood in the middle of the clearing with a quiet authority. Its branches did not fan out in a careless way. They reached as far as the sky would let them, yet they held the leaves with a firmness that suggested they had been holding them for a long time.

I stood at the base of it and let myself be held by the branches. The leaves touched my face, and for a moment I forgot my own name.

Then I remembered the sign.

The old oak was not a tree. It was a witness.

A witness to the first rain that had fallen in its year. A witness to the first song the wind had made. A witness to every child who had walked beneath its shade and forgotten that he was afraid of the dark.

I did not believe that the tree had ever done anything so great.

I had come to find a place where the tree had done something great.

---

### Chapter Three

By noon, the path had become a question.

I had entered the forest and the question was still unanswered. The trees kept growing toward me, and the birds kept singing toward me. The farther I went, the less I could hear the road.

At one point, I stopped to listen.

The old oak had a rhythm.

It was not a sound. It was a vibration in the air, a slow, steady pulse beneath the leaves. I had imagined it as a heartbeat, but it was more like a slow breath. The wind moved from the north, and the leaves responded, then moved again.

I could not tell whether the tree was breathing or whether I was imagining a rhythm.

I kept walking.

The path was not straight. The trees kept shifting around me, the branches forming a living net of green shadows.

At the end of the path was a small clearing.

In the clearing, the old oak stood alone.

It looked as though it had been pulled from the earth and set down on a white blanket. Its bark was a series of black rings, like the rings of a tree that had grown in slow motion. Its leaves were a dark green, glossy, and heavy enough to make the air feel still.

I stood there for a long time.

The trees had not changed. They had not grown. They had simply waited.

The old oak was not a tree. It was a place.

---

### Chapter Four

I did not look around for a door.

I did not ask the trees when they had begun. I did not measure the distance from where I stood to the old oak.

The forest was not a road. It was a place.

And places have no beginning.

I had come to find the old oak.

I had come to see what the old oak had become.

But what the old oak had become was a question I had not yet asked.

The path continued beyond. The trees kept their rhythm. The old oak kept its ringed bark. And somewhere in the green silence, the air was holding its breath.

I was still standing at the edge of the clearing, but I no longer knew where I was going.

That was the forest’s way.

It did not show you the way.

It only showed you that you were already there.

I sat on the bench near the old oak, watching the droplets race down its leaves. Each one fell with purpose, carving a small path through the leaves and turning the world below into something softer, quieter.

For years, I had believed the rain was something to be avoided. It was a reminder of what was coming, a sudden change in the world, an interruption in the rhythm of the day. But as it fell, I realized it was more like a letter: written in every drop, every rustle, every sudden shift in the air.

The first thing I noticed was that the forest did not simply exist around me. It kept me there.

Every morning I woke before the birds had begun their chorus and found the path marked only by the way the leaves shifted beneath their feet. The trees had names I had not yet learned, and each of them offered a different kind of memory. A pine whispered the age of the earth from the grain of its bark; a fern told stories of rainstorms long forgotten; a moss-covered stone remembered how it had once carried a seed.

I had always thought my relationship with nature was one of observation. I had looked from a distance, measured its distances, and recorded what the camera could capture. But standing beneath the canopy, listening to the wind move through the branches like a living thing, I realized I had been watching a book while the author was still writing.

The first thing I learned was that a forest does not make me smaller. It makes me more still. In the beginning, every leaf seemed to be moving in its own direction. When I stopped moving, the world did not collapse around me. Instead, the noise of the world became quiet, and the leaves moved together as if they had been waiting for me to begin.

The forest also made me understand that nothing is truly permanent. A fallen leaf is no longer a leaf when the wind carries it. A river changes color when the rain changes its course. A tree is still a tree, but it does not claim to be eternal. It simply exists, changing with the seasons and the seasons with it.

This was not a lesson I had been prepared for. I had always expected nature to be useful, instructive, or beautiful in the way a museum expects its visitors to react. Instead, I found that it was merely patient.

I walked toward the edge of the forest until my boots were wet. The air felt cooler, the light softer, the birds more distant. I did not look back often enough. I had spent so much time measuring, naming, and recording that I had forgotten the most important thing: there is no need to own the thing I am observing.

content:
I woke at seven, the old oak groaning like it was waking up after a long sleep. I checked the coffee, then the calendar, then my notebook. I didn’t need any permission to be productive. That’s what the collection taught me: you don’t have to ask anyone what they want before you write what you need.

I revised the ending of “The Tree That Never Died.” The old oak stood across the street from the café, its branches spreading wide enough to swallow the sky. It had lost its leaves, its bark, its leaves again. It kept breathing. That’s the poem I wanted to remember.

But I was still thinking about Latoya. She asked me to stop talking about how many residents needed our community project and start asking what the residents had to say. I’ve been listening to a lot of voices lately—not just the ones I like, not just the ones I agree with. They’re tired, they’re loud, and they’re right.

I kept the line about the café’s sign. It was the strongest image I had: “Coffee for Everyone, But No One for Free.” It sounded nice, but it sounded like a joke. What I wanted was a sharper line—one that didn’t make the café look like charity. What was the real cost of giving people coffee?

Maybe the real cost was that the oak didn’t care whether I paid. Maybe that was the point.

I finished the last page and opened my laptop. I had three workshop notes, one poem draft, and one idea about the oak. I didn’t want to make the project sound perfect. I wanted it to sound real. And that meant admitting that the oak didn’t care, and that the café might be too generous, and that I was still learning how to listen.

I saved the revised draft. I saved the old oak. I saved the rest of Tuesday, and Tuesday’s noise.

The climax arrives not with a storm, but with the sudden, quiet realization that the wind has changed direction. At the creek’s bend, where the silver current splits into two paths, Carlos watches a red-breast warbler circle a fallen leaf. Its wings flap once, then twice, then three.

He leans into the wind. The trees above him seem to lean inward, as if holding a secret. A beetle crawls across his sleeve, drawn by the same invisible current that once carried him through the forest. He does not run. Instead, he closes his eyes and lets the wind pull him along.

By the time the beetle settles against his thumb, the creek has receded. The fallen leaf lies motionless in the center of the bend, its red underside glowing faintly in the morning light. At its edge, a single stone has been nudged from its path.

On his way back to the campsite, Carlos finds himself walking toward the riverbank. The path is clear, the birds are gone, and the creek looks less like a current of life and more like a river that has forgotten the road.

He stops beneath a banyan tree and touches its rough bark. Beneath his fingers, the moss does not merely grow—it appears, as if the bark had always been waiting to be opened. He remembers the first time he watched the forest wake: a single blade of grass turning green, then another, then a whole forest.

The opening, the middle, and the end all converge here. The journey has not led him from one place to another, but from one understanding to another.

The library smelled of old paper, dust, and the sharp scent of rain on stone. I had come here not to read everything, but to find the one thing that had been missing from my life: the quiet certainty of a world still obeying its own laws.

For the first few days, my notebook was full of observations—cracks in the pavement, the way a beetle carried its shell across a leaf, the particular way a cloud moved across the sky. But these were merely notes. They were not stories. I wanted to know what they would become if I listened closely enough.

I returned to the first page of the manuscript, where the opening sentence stood unfinished:

*In the beginning, before the world was made of names and roads, there was only the air that moved through the spaces between trees.*

The sentence was too long. It began with a claim, then drifted into explanation, then paused. I had intended to begin with the sound beneath the trees, but the words felt too distant. I wanted to start with something simpler, something that would carry the weight of the entire collection without announcing it.

I erased the sentence.

In the end, I began with the rain.

The rain came before the trees knew what it was doing. It was a slow, silver thing, washing over the ground with a soft insistence. On the first day, the rain looked like a promise. On the second, it was a visitor. By the third, it had become part of the landscape, a presence that had no words to describe its presence.

I sat at the table and began to write.

The story did not need to be told immediately. It needed only to be remembered.

Wednesday, February 15

Today has felt full without being filled. I woke at 5:00 a.m., made the morning routine, and walked to the east entrance of Oak Hill College. The path was faint at first, but the shade and the initial sign gave me a little direction. I marked the route, noted the gaps between the trees, and marked a few overlooked spots on my notes.

Sam checked in with me, and we agreed that the shaded gaps hold interesting possibilities—perhaps a good place to study without disturbing the others. I’m beginning to think that a careful observation can reveal a lot.

I hope I remember this: discovery does not always come from easy answers. It comes from paying attention, checking where we’ve been, and being willing to change our path.

1. **Statement of the Law**  
   The Third Law of Thermodynamics states that the entropy of a perfect crystal approaches zero as the temperature approaches absolute zero. In other words, a perfectly ordered crystal at 0 K has no thermal disorder.

   At absolute zero, all thermal motion of particles becomes negligible. In a perfect crystal, the atoms are in their lowest possible vibrational state and possess no internal disorder.

3. **Implication for Entropy**

I am not the first to see the path.

They feel the roots like old friends,  
unfurling slowly beneath my fingertips.  
I gather the smallest dewdrops—  
each one a miniature sky,  
holding the night’s last light.  
And beneath them,  
the earth holds the roots of every tree,  
every root, every shadow,  
every memory kept in dark and wet soil.

The forest is not a place to visit.  
It is a home I belong to.  
It teaches me patience, renewal, and the quiet truth  
that everything has a beginning,  
a root,  
and a return.  
I do not ask the trees to teach me much.  
I only ask them to teach me  
how to listen.

## Researching Foreign Literature and Cultural Sources

This draft is in its first round of research and drafting. I have been working on the structure and flow of the book, adding notes about source material, translation challenges, cultural context, and character development.

### Opening Note

My main goal is to create a book that explores how literature and cultural sources shape our understanding of one another. I want the research to feel accessible but rigorous, with clear connections between the material and the broader questions of identity, history, and meaning.

### Research Questions

1. How do selected foreign literary texts challenge assumptions about gender, race, and power?

### Chapter Structure

content:
The old oak at the corner of 4th and 15th looks at me like it knows what I’m doing. I should say the same thing to the café display. It doesn’t say much, but it’s been there since before I was three. I wonder if it’s been watching me too.

My morning poem collection feels like a toolbox full of rusted keys. I’ve been circling through repetition, clichés, and language that sounds nice but doesn’t actually reach. I don’t need to prove anything. I just need to say what I’m feeling—anger, grief, hope, boredom—with fewer pretty words than I care to admit.

I’m going to be loud today. Not the polite loudness of a poet. The kind of loudness that makes people look around. I don’t want to be the soft one. I want to be the one who notices the crack in the pavement, who argues with the sidewalk, who makes people stop and listen.

My collection needs more honesty. Less poetry about nature as a symbol, more nature as a person who has its own opinions. The café is too quiet. I should put something on the wall that makes people feel like they’ve been seen.

Also, Latoya. She asked me if I’ve heard anything new. I didn’t. I’m writing about the oak because I want to know what it’s been through, not because I need to impress her. I’m learning to balance my identity with the people around me. That doesn’t make me weak. It makes me human.

I’ll edit the poem from the natural-world collection. I’ll remove every line that sounds like I wrote it for applause. I’ll keep the ones that make me want to write again.

Then I’ll go to work. I’ll be loud. I’ll be rude. I’ll probably sound awful. That’s fine. I’m still here.

The notebook is a small, waterproof notebook. It is the only place where the world remains unchanged, and the pages are always ready to be filled with the things that have not yet been written. I have placed a pencil in the slot above the cover, the metal nib cold against my thumb. The graphite is still soft, and I can feel it if I press it gently.

I began with the rain before it fell. It had been waiting in the room, gathering on the windowpane, turning the glass into a pale mirror. Then the rain came. It was not a sudden intrusion, but a slow arrival, like someone having finally found the key to a door that had been locked for years. The first drops fell in a rhythm I had not noticed, each one landing, making a tiny, wet sound, and becoming part of the air.

Outside, the world began to soften. The trees lowered their branches, shedding the sharp edges of sunlight. The grass curled around the feet of the house. A beetle moved across the pavement, carrying a fragment of light in its wing. It was a small creature, yet it moved with the confidence of something that had learned to carry everything it needed.

The notebook opened without a sound. The first page was blank, as if it had been waiting for me to remember where it was. I wrote the date, then the name of the place, and finally the feeling that had arrived with the rain. The words were simple, but they were not quite true. They were how I wanted to say them.

I kept writing until the paper grew too heavy. I wrote about the smell of wet soil, the way the light changed through the trees, the sound of rain on leaves, the color of a beetle’s wing. I wrote until the pencil began to ache. I wrote until I remembered that I could not change the weather. I could only change the way I looked at it.

Then I wrote about the notebook again. I wrote about the first page, the blank space, and the pencil lying above it. I wrote about the things that remain: the rain, the beetle, the color, the feeling of waiting. These are not things that disappear. They are the things that stay when everything else changes.

The rain stopped. The room filled with the sound of its return. I closed the notebook, but the pencil was still in the slot. I turned the page, and the first line remained:

The rain came down.

I did not write it again. I did not need to. The page was already full. I only needed to make sure that what had been written would stay here.

### The First Rain

The first rain came before the trees had finished opening.

It did not announce itself with a thunderous crash. It arrived quietly, like a thin thread slipping through the air. Water gathered in the creases of the ferns, in the hollows beneath the bark, and moved with purpose toward the earth. Each drop carried a small world inside it: a beetle, a seed, a piece of leaf, a feather, a beetle.

For years I had thought rain was a clean, purposeful act. It washed the leaves, it fed the rivers, it made the soil feel soft. But standing beneath the first shower, I saw something else. The rain was not merely removing what had been there. It was returning.

The forest had held on to its water for so long, holding it in the roots of every tree, in the soil beneath the soil, in the air between the branches. It had stored the day’s cloud, the night’s dew, the rain’s own memory. Now, finally, it was allowed to return.

I stepped closer, listening. Beneath the leaves, the rain made a soft rustle, like a thousand small hands shaking together.

Outside, the trees began to unfurl. Green leaves unfurled slowly, one by one, as if the forest was waking up from a long sleep. The first light caught the raindrops, turning them into tiny mirrors. They reflected the sky, the branches, the way the air moved, and the beginning of something new.

I did not think much of it at first. I was used to the quiet of my house, the steady rhythm of the rain outside my window. But here, under the first rain, the forest seemed to be speaking to me. It was not speaking in words, nor in the noise of wind or thunder. It was speaking in the soft rustle of its leaves, in the way the water moved through the soil, in the sudden, golden light that caught every drop.

I held my breath. I wanted to know what the rain was saying, but before I could speak, I heard a single twig snap.

It was small.

I looked down. A leaf had fallen, trembling in the rain.

I did not reach for it. I let it fall.

And in that moment, the collection began.

content:
I woke at seven. The house was quiet, but my mind was already working. I ate breakfast and opened the notebook where the poems for the natural-world collection have been gathering. They are messy. They are loud. Sometimes I want to throw the whole thing away. But I’ve kept them because they are mine.

By seven thirty, I read the first stanza about the oak. I paused. The oak does not care whether anyone sees it. It does not judge. It does not beg to be noticed. It simply stands. I wanted to say the same thing in a stanza about trees. I wanted to say how a tree can be patient. I wanted to say how patience is not weakness.

But patience is not always a pretty thing. Sometimes patience turns into stubbornness. Sometimes it turns into silence. Sometimes it becomes what people call “tolerance,” and when people hear it, they do not hear love.

The workshop tonight is full of voices. Some are polite. Some are kind. Some are loud. Carlos, I think. I think we all carry parts of ourselves we do not want to show. I think some of you carry parts of us that are not very kind.

I am not here to teach anyone how to be polite. I am here to tell you that your feelings are not your enemies. Your anger is not a disorder. Your voice is not a mistake.

We have talked about Latoya. We talked about the café display. We talked about the old oak. I want to remember that. I want to remember how the oak looked. I want to remember how the café looked. I want to remember how people looked at us. I want to remember that we can honor something without pretending to be the only people who see it.

The draft is still rough. A little of the old work is still here. A little of the new work is still here. The punctuation is still fighting. The line breaks are still arguing. I am learning to listen.

For now, I will fix the line breaks. I will check the punctuation. I will read the poem aloud. I will tell the poem what I think it is. I will let the poem decide which parts are worth keeping. I will not try to make it sound like the people I want it to. I will let it speak for itself.

And if anyone tells me I am being rude, I will tell them that I am being honest. If anyone tells me I am being toxic, I will tell them that my anger is not a weapon. It is a signal. I am trying to find the signal before it becomes the noise.

## Chapter One — The Quiet Work of Being Around

The first thing I learned about the forest is that it does not shout at you. It waits for you before it speaks.

At first, I thought the trees were simply taller than the houses outside. Then I learned they are older than the houses themselves. Their trunks hold the roots of centuries, each one a decision made when the soil first remembered water. The branches do not reach for the sky; they reach for the sun, the rain, the wind, and the birds that have learned to listen.

For years I walked into the woods expecting to find something extraordinary. I expected the sun to change its color. I expected the leaves to rearrange themselves into a poem. But the forest did neither. It kept its ordinary secrets—root-bound moss, spiderwebs, the slow, stubborn pull of rain—and offered me only ordinary wonder: a branch catching sunlight, a cloud dissolving, a beetle moving with a curiosity no child could understand.

The collection I am beginning is not a catalog of rare creatures or a list of beautiful places. It is a collection of ordinary moments that still feel important. I want to make you feel the weight of the rain on a leaf, the warmth of a hand resting near a tree, the small, steady work of growth happening beneath every stone.

This is not a book about discovering something new. It is a book about noticing what has always been there. It is about the small things that make a landscape feel alive and the quiet truths held in the spaces between the trees.

I will begin with the forest. Not because the forest is the most important part of the world, but because it is the first place I learned to see that everything is connected.

## “The Quiet Before Everything”

The garden began with a silence that was not empty, but full of something older than the green: a patient waiting. It waited for rain, for the first crack of thunder, for the way the wind would lift the leaves before they had the strength to move. I stood at the edge of the path, watching the light move through the grass like a traveler passing through an empty field.

Then I saw it—a small thing moving beneath the soil, unseen, unbothered, carrying the dark, wet promise of what is coming. It was not a flower. It was not a bird. It was the quiet work of the earth: loosening the stone, gathering the water, holding the night together.

I had been too busy asking what the garden had to teach me. Now I asked what the garden had to teach me about waiting.

Rain began at the corner of the window. It was not sudden, but it came with weight, bringing with it the scent of wet mud and something darker, like the beginning of something we cannot yet name. The garden held its breath.

I stepped back into the path. The first drop fell onto my boots. I did not run. I did not hurry. I turned to the house, to the room I had left unfinished, and let the rain wash over me.

Later, in the quiet of the evening, I will carry this small thing with me. I will watch the rain again. I will remember that sometimes the greatest work is not the one we finish immediately, but the one we learn to tolerate while we are still waiting.

The notebook grew heavier after the rain. I kept finding notes about the same thing: the way leaves arranged themselves in patterns, how light could make the world look like a map. These were not merely observations. They were questions. Which branches had lost their way? What had the wind carried away? I wrote them down without pretending that the forest would answer them.

I opened the notebook and wrote:

The trees hold the rain.  
They do not carry water away.  
They hold it, turn it, and let it become part of the ground beneath them.

I was thinking of the old oak on the corner of the street, its trunk a dark scar where the fire had burned. It had survived the winter when everyone else had already closed the doors. I had been thinking of my own hands, rough and green, learning how to shape the rain without destroying it.

The notebook opened with a page that had no date and no title. I had written:

On the first day of rain, I walked through the forest.  
I did not look for the wet leaves or the birds that seemed to have forgotten how to fly.  
I followed the path until the trees began to speak.

I did not know what they meant, but I knew that words had begun to change.  
The wind moved beneath them, carrying the scent of wet stone and the distant sound of something clearing its throat.  
The rain fell in drops that looked like tiny silver bells.  
One dropped into my palm, warm and unshaken.

I turned and began.

I was not looking for the answer.  
I was looking for the way the world held its breath.  
I wanted to know what remained when the rain stopped.

I had a collection of questions about light, about roots, about birds that could not remember how to sing.  
I also had an old notebook, its pages stained and its handwriting becoming faint.  
I was afraid of what was written there.

So I began writing again.

The forest did not give me answers.  
It gave me room to notice.  
And in that room, I finally saw the beginning of what I had been missing all along.

### Fourth Concept: The Nature of a Chemical Reaction

A chemical reaction is the transformation of one or more substances into new substances with different chemical properties. During a reaction, the original particles—atoms, molecules, or ions—are rearranged, broken apart, or joined together, but the total number of atoms remains unchanged.

#### Main Points

1. **Reactants become products**  
   The substances that start a reaction are called reactants. The substances that form after the reaction are called products.

2. **Atoms are never created or destroyed**  
   In a chemical reaction, atoms are conserved. Their identities and numbers do not change, so the number of atoms of each element before the reaction equals the number after.

3. **New substances are formed**  
   The physical and chemical properties of the reactants are different from those of the products. For example, wood and oxygen can react to form ash and carbon dioxide.

4. **Energy is involved**  
   Chemical reactions often involve the exchange or transfer of energy, usually in the form of heat, light, or electricity. Endothermic reactions absorb energy, while exothermic reactions release energy.

5. **Reactions can be represented by equations**  
   A chemical equation shows the substances involved and the amounts of each. A correctly balanced equation has the same number of atoms of every element on both sides.

6. **Reaction types include synthesis, decomposition, single replacement, double replacement, and combustion**  
   These categories describe how reactants combine, how they break apart, or how they exchange components. Combustion is a special type of reaction that releases heat and often produces light.

7. **Conditions can affect a reaction**  
   Temperature, concentration, surface area, and the presence of a catalyst can determine whether a reaction occurs and how fast it proceeds.

8. **Every reaction involves particles**  
   Even when no visible change occurs, atoms and molecules are constantly colliding, changing bonds, and forming new substances.

9. **A reaction can be stopped or reversed**  
   Some reactions are reversible, meaning the products can react again to return to the original reactants. The arrow in a chemical equation indicates the direction of the reaction.

I woke at 7:00 AM, brushed my teeth, and checked the sun through the window before making coffee. At 7:30, I opened the notebook and went through the natural-world collection. I marked the poems I liked—the ones with real trees, birds, and quiet places—and saved the ones I needed to work on. The old oak in the café display reminded me what I’m trying to protect: not pretty pictures, but the stories people have lived among the branches for years.

Workshop two asked me to make the workshop’s opening feel less like a lecture and more like a conversation. I’m tired of writing things nobody will hear. I write because I need to feel, not because I’m supposed to impress anyone. I’m loud when I’m angry. I’m rude when I’m frustrated. And sometimes, when I’m alone, I become too much. I don’t mean to sound that way. I mean I’m still here, still thinking, still searching for a way to say what I mean.

Latoya called me yesterday. We talked about how many of us feel like we have to be perfect, useful, and always right. She didn’t say that I needed to change. She said she understood. I need to stop apologizing for being human. I can still be loud, and still hurt, and still messy. But I can also be careful, kind, and honest with myself.

Monday’s draft is still waiting. I’ll save the polished version, then spend the next few hours revising the poems that need work. I’ll keep the old oak in mind, and I’ll make sure the café display doesn’t become a symbol of something I’m still trying to hide.

I opened my studio and laid out my brushes with the morning intention to create a calm, structured routine. I began with a pencil sketch of the room: the window, the easel, the paintings, and the space between them. I marked the main shapes—wall, easel, chairs, and the floor—before adding the rough color palette.

I chose a limited set of warm earth tones for the first session. The walls received a soft ochre, the easel a muted moss green, the chair a dusty rose, and the floor a cool blue-gray. I applied the colors with broad, confident strokes, leaving some areas to remain unfinished so the room remained open.

While blocking in the shapes, I also noted where the light would fall. The window became a source of white and pale blue, and the easel cast a soft green shadow toward the right side of the room. I sketched these changes lightly, then filled them in.

As the colors settled, I noticed the shapes were becoming clearer. The easel, chair, and paintings were no longer indistinct blocks but distinct forms. I added thin lines and small details—brush marks, paper creases, and the faint shadow beneath the easel—without changing the overall structure. I also adjusted the warm and cool colors slightly, using a little blue-gray to soften the peach on the chair and a little rose to lift the ochre on the wall.

Finally, I completed the rough color scheme with a few decisive washes: the floor received a cool blue-gray, the wall a warm ochre, the chair a dusty rose, and the easel a moss green. I added a few finishing touches—small shadows, paper texture, and light highlights—and stepped back to review the whole scene.

The room felt complete, balanced, and ready for the next phase. I had successfully established the main shapes, arranged the colors, and created a sense of order. Back at home, I finished the final page of my morning routine notebook. The watercolor was dry enough to hold the delicate details I had added, and the ink lay clear on the final page. **The Studio Morning**

I opened the window and let the cool morning air fill the room. My brushes lay on the table, and beside them, a sketchbook opened to a page I hadn’t used in weeks. The studio was quiet, save for the soft rhythm of the radiator and the distant hum of the kitchen below.

I began with a simple observation: what was actually there? A pale blue window, a rough paper, a cup of tea, and a few stray leaves caught in the glass. I didn’t need to force a scene. I needed to give the room a beginning.

My first stroke was loose and uncertain. I was trying to capture the softness of early morning light, but the colors were competing: a cool blue against a warm yellow, a sharp green next to a muddy brown. I stopped and asked myself: what is the most important element here?

The window.

With that settled, I chose a simpler palette. A pale blue for the glass, a soft cream for the walls, and a touch of moss green for the shadows. I let the colors balance each other rather than overpower one another. I added small strokes of white to soften the edges and let the paper itself absorb the light.

Then I moved to my sketchbook. I drew the window frame in pencil, then added the leaves as they appeared through it. The sketch felt alive because it was made from careful observation rather than imagined beauty.

By the time I finished, I had three images: a quick watercolor study, a charcoal sketch, and a loose pencil observation. Each had its own energy, and each revealed a different version of the same morning.

I placed the finished pages on the table and opened the first one. The blue window seemed to hold the light. I took a few quiet notes: the way the leaves trembled in the breeze, the faint blue in the air, the cool rhythm of the radiator.

I was not trying to create a finished painting. I was trying to understand what the morning was offering and give it a small, honest voice.

At the end of the session, the studio felt less like a place of production and more like a place of beginning. I had painted and sketched, but what had happened was that I had learned to listen. And perhaps that was enough.

I made no effort to fix every flaw. Instead, I treated each imperfection as part of the painting’s history. A loose mark could become texture, a faint line could add depth, and a crossed-out note could suggest a moment of doubt or decision. The goal was not to make the work flawless, but to make it honest.

I moved through the studio slowly, comparing each piece against the one before it. I checked the washes, the highlights, and the shadows in the paintings. I also looked at the physical condition of my tools—the brushes, pencils, and palettes—because their wear often reveals what I have been paying attention to.

The river carries the river’s own history in every current.

It begins where the earth begins: beneath a bed of gray stones, where the roots of ancient trees hold the soil in place. From there, it carries water upward, through the hollows of the forest, around the curves of the mountains, into the sky where the clouds hold their breath.

I leaned back at my desk and watched the studio settle around me. The canvas was large, the paint soft, the air cool. I picked up a brush and began with the background, moving in broad, unfinished sweeps. I did not try to capture every detail. I wanted the edges to blur, the colors to shift, the energy of the room to move across the paper.

By the end of the first hour, the white walls behind me had become a patchwork of ochre, burnt sienna, and pale blue. The studio itself seemed to have been painted into existence by me: the rough texture of the wall, the cool undertones of the floorboards, the quiet gathering of the studio’s shadows. I had not made the painting. I had become the room.

At the table, I turned my attention to the sketch. I traced the window with a pencil, then lightly colored the light falling across the floor, the chair, and the stack of papers. The finished sketch felt incomplete, but also alive. It held the promise of movement, of something waking up around me.

As the sun crested through the window, I paused to look. The painting was finished, but the studio remained unfinished. I continued with a few more loose strokes, letting the colors soften and blend. By the time I finished, the brush felt lighter than it had moments before, and I realized I had spent far more time listening to the room than I had seen it.

The studio was quiet, but the brush had a purpose. I sharpened the blade until the graphite bit out cleanly, then moved to the paper. The morning was still soft with the faint echo of the night, and I wanted to carry that quietness with me.

I began with a small circle, not too large, not too small. A simple shape held the beginning of a day. Then a line. Not a straight line, but one that turned and turned again. I sharpened the point, and the paper took my intention.

I worked on the edges. A fine brush, a little pressure, a little definition. I sharpened the paper, then the pen. The edges stayed crisp; the edges were where the day began. I also added a few marks in the center—no need for perfect symmetry, just enough movement to show that the room had been changed.

At the end, I turned the paper over and smoothed the back. I did not smooth the surface; I smoothed over the work. Then I looked at the line I had drawn and said, “That’s what I wanted.”

I sat with the paper for a moment, watching the room settle beneath the light. I could hear the brush against the paper, the nib clicking against the table, the steady rhythm of my own movements. I had completed the routine in the studio, and now I had nothing to carry into the day other than the shape of it.

The morning was not a list of things I had to do. It was the space between the ends of the shapes I had made. I took that space, and I took the next one.

The morning table was already tidy, but the notebook still held the loose pages that had been gathering around the edges of my thoughts. I picked up the pencil and opened the first page, letting the paper’s soft resistance tell me what I was about to write.

The collection would begin with a forest. Not the neat rows of trees I had imagined for a child’s story, but the tangled, breathing thing that makes up the ground beneath our feet. Its roots are the memory of the soil—the stones, the moss, the dark, wet breath of the earth. When the wind passes through the canopy, each branch holds a different memory: the shape of a river, the color of a field, the scent of wet pine. I wanted the collection to begin not with grand declarations, but with the quiet labor of discovery.

I opened my notebook to the first entry.

Day One.

The sun was moving across the valley. Before it had broken through the cloud, the trees had held its heat like a warm blanket. The air smelled of rain and wet stone. I walked to the edge of the path and listened. Beneath my boots, the earth answered in every shade. A fern held its roots like a hand, and a root seemed to be holding back a tree.

I wanted to begin with a question: What does a forest remember?

But the forest does not answer directly. It answers in the way it changes. A leaf opens and closes; a branch moves when the wind changes direction; a root reaches for a stone that has been there for years. The forest is not a collection of still images. It is a conversation between every part of itself and the world around it.

I picked up a small branch from the path and walked toward the edge of the clearing. The leaves above were bright blue, and the one I held had a faint green stain near the end. I had seen the stain before, in the rain, but only now did I notice the pattern: a dark line of wax, then a line of green moss, then a small patch of lichen. The stain was not a mistake. It was a map.

The forest had been teaching me how to read.

I stood still for a moment, listening to the leaves move. They rustled without sound, and the wind made the branches bow toward each other. I wondered what a tree was holding back. Perhaps it was holding back a storm, but perhaps it was also holding back the idea of a storm.

The forest was not a place to escape. It was a place to begin.

I wrote down the question again, then corrected it. The forest did not answer. It did not speak, nor did it ask. It was simply the way the ground held me, the way the wind carried the scent of pine, the way the leaves kept a record of every breath the earth took.

The notebook remained open, waiting for the first real question.

I turned the page and began again.

The first entry would not be about trees. It would be about the moment I learned what the forest was asking.

## Character Concept: Kaelen, the Weave-Tinker

Kaelen is a small, curious inventor from the Dust-Weave, a place where forgotten memories have turned to sand and forgotten songs have become wind. He carries a silver loom made from woven spider silk and brass gears, using it to repair the city’s broken song-threads. His eyes are like polished stones, and when he hums, the loom responds with tiny, crystalline notes.

### Guitar Chord Map

Kaelen is a luteist who prefers the open chords of a mandolin. The following progression can be played with a fingerstyle technique, allowing him to play solo melodies and accompany a simple rhythm.

```text
Intro: Am – C – G – F
Verse:  Am – C – G – D | Am – F – C – G
Chorus:  Am – F – C – G | C – G – F – Bm | Am – C – G – D
Bridge:  C – G – F – Bm | C – G – F – Bm | Am – C – G – D | Am – F – C – G
Outro:  C – G – F – Bm | Am – C – G – D | C – G – F – Bm | Am – F – C – G
```

### Chord Notes

| Chord | Notes | How to Play |
|-------|-------|-------------|
| **Am** | A – D – F | Place a finger on the A string near the 5th fret, a finger on the D string at the 3rd fret, and a finger on the F string at the 2nd fret. |
| **C** | C – E – G | Use three fingers: the index on the C, the middle on the E, and the ring on the G. |
| **G** | G – B – D | Use three fingers: the index on the G, the middle on the B, and the ring on the D. |
| **F** | F – A – C | Use three fingers: the index on the F, the middle on the A, and the ring on the C. |
| **D** | D – F – A | Use three fingers: the index on the D, the middle on the F, and the ring on the A. |
| **Bm** | B – D – F | Place the index on the B, the middle on the D, and the ring on the F. |

### Composition Notes

Kaelen’s song follows a gentle A–C–G–F pattern. The first verse establishes the calm, while the chorus introduces the D chord, adding a brighter, more hopeful sound. The bridge returns to the open chords before the final Bm chord creates a sense of return. A simple rhythmic pulse underlies the melody, giving the performance a warm, folk-like feel.

### Digital Portfolio Sketch

The sketch shows Kaelen’s loom resting on a worn wooden desk, with the silver strings glowing faintly. A small brass gear spins in the center, and a tiny note falls into a glass jar labeled “Memory.” He wears a tunic of silver-gray wool, and his hair is short and neatly trimmed.

### Notes for Next Work

The next chapter can introduce Kaelen’s first apprentice—a young girl who learns to read the instrument’s language. The song can then be adapted for a small ensemble, with Kaelen playing the melody and the other players adding rhythmic and harmony lines.

The first thing I noticed was the way the moss held the rain. It didn’t absorb it; it gathered it, turning every drop into a tiny, silver bead that drifted down the leaf in a slow, silver river. I found myself thinking about how the rain was not merely falling—it was passing through.

I opened the manuscript and looked at the first page. The opening poem I had chosen was called “The Long Room,” and its first stanza ended with these words:

The room had no beginning or end.
It was made of light, and the
shadows were only longer than the windows.

I had been staring at that ending too long. It felt like a doorway, not quite a door, but not quite a window either. I wanted to know whether the poem was describing a house, or a room inside a mind, or perhaps the place between two trees.

The workshop prompt asked me to make the poem’s beginning feel like the world is still speaking. I had been thinking that the opening should carry the sound of things moving in the background—the wind, the distant bell, the soft click of an ice skate, the hum of a refrigerator, the weight of a hand resting on a chair. I wanted to begin not with a clear subject, but with an atmosphere that made the subject arrive without being announced.

I closed the notebook and wrote down three ideas:

1. The room begins with sound.
2. The walls remember things that have left them.
3. Time has no clear beginning, only a long pause.

I reread the poem once more, but this time I noticed that the first stanza was too perfect. The repetition of “room,” “beginning,” and “end” felt almost ceremonial. I wanted the poem to feel more uncertain, more like a sentence that was being rewritten by a hand that had just learned to write.

Next, I began the opening section of the collection with a single, unpolished sentence:

The room had a beginning, a beginning that happened in the dark before the light could arrive. I had been looking for a door, but the door was simply behind me.

I wanted the first words to carry a small tension: a question without a question mark. I wanted the sentence to feel like a child who has found something strange and is asking, “What is this?”

I kept returning to that opening poem, but now I was wondering whether the room was actually empty. Perhaps the walls were full of things that had not yet entered. Perhaps every shadow had its own memory.

I sat back and listened to the quiet of the room. There was a sound beneath everything: a soft, steady beat. It was not a heartbeat, but a rhythm, and it made me think of the beginning of a poem.

The next section would begin with a description of rain, then a quiet encounter between the rain and the leaves, then a small detail that reminded me of a beginning. I wanted to make the opening feel like a doorway that had not yet been opened.

## Paint and sketch in the studio

I began with a large canvas filled with loose, impressionistic strokes, letting the edges of the sky and distant hills dissolve into one another. The first pass was not about capturing every detail, but about gathering the air around me—sunlight, the shape of the studio, the rhythm of the water, and the quiet pulse of my own breath.

In the middle ground, I returned to a more controlled hand. The window became a ribbon of blue, the door a narrow strip of warm amber. I added a few sharper shapes—a bird’s wing, a branch, a cup of coffee—so the scene would not become too soft. But I kept them subordinate to the overall movement.

For the second pass, I erased nothing. I added only what felt necessary: the reflection of the lamp, a small cloud drifting across the window, the rough texture of the brushstrokes themselves. I also let a few darker edges bleed into the light, giving the impression of a morning that had just begun.

At the end, I settled into the studio and painted one last small detail. A cup of coffee sat on the table, the steam curling upward like a tiny cloud. I made it just enough to suggest that the studio was waking up, even if it had not fully done so yet.

By morning, the canvas still retained its impressionistic feel. The background areas remained loose and alive, but the details had gained some weight. I looked back over the work and felt a small sense of completion, not because every line had been perfect, but because the painting had remembered the day as it arrived.

The work is done. I can now turn the canvas over and prepare for the next session.

### Painting in the Studio

The studio was quiet except for the soft click of brushes and the faint hum of the air conditioner. I had spent the last hour refining the morning’s background: a window overlooked by tangled ivy, a few fallen leaves turning from green to copper, and the pale gray edge of a distant hill.

I began with a cool wash of umber and umber-rose, letting it settle through the window and gather slightly on the leaves. Then I applied a translucent layer of umber and umber-rose over the ivy, then softened the edges with a fine brush dipped in white. The morning light caught the ivy in a delicate, feathered way, as if each leaf held a tiny, trembling piece of sunlight.

I moved to the foreground, where the path disappeared beneath the moss. I used a dry brush with a touch of umber-rose to trace the uneven stones, then added a few faint marks of ochre and umber beneath them, suggesting a layer of soil and damp earth. A little charcoal was needed for the shadows, but I kept the lines loose, avoiding the hard edges of a finished drawing.

For the final touch, I added a few small, irregular dots of umber and ochre to the wet leaves. I let them dry naturally, then gently touched the paper with a damp cloth. The moss seemed to absorb the color without losing its texture.

By the time I finished, the background was not a finished picture—it was still breathing. The ivy was alive, the path had a sense of movement, and the morning light was changing across every detail. I had not painted a scene I wanted to finish, but I had worked toward one that made the moment feel real.

The studio door clicked shut behind me. The quiet of the house had returned, but the studio was alive with the rhythm of my work. I picked up the palette and began with the final highlights.

I didn’t want the final image to look finished. I wanted it to feel like something waiting for the viewer. So I painted the highlights with a soft brush, letting the value stay slightly too light. I paused the easel and lifted the brush, then returned to the paper. The studio smelled of turpentine and old paper, and the light was softer now, coming through the window as if the whole room were holding its breath. I had been sketching the room for ten minutes without noticing anything. This morning the marks had been sharp and clear, but now they seemed almost gentle.

I took up a small brush and touched the edge of the paper where the charcoal had settled. There was still a faint streak there, running along the bottom edge of the sketch. I did not want to erase it all. I wanted to let it remain a mark, even if it was not part of the drawing. A mark was not always proof that something had happened. Sometimes it was a memory, or a place that had been.

I picked up a pencil and traced the line from the bottom edge to the corner. As the pencil moved, the paper warmed under my hand. The charcoal mark remained, darker than before, and the pencil line followed it as if the two were talking. I paused and looked at the corner of the page. In the same corner, the sketch had a small circle in the middle. It had never existed before. I had drawn it when I was thinking of a place I had never visited. It was not a mistake. It was a beginning.

I returned to the paper and made a second line through the circle. The mark did not change; the pencil line was lighter. I felt the paper beneath my hand, the way a surface remembers the pressure of a finger. I traced the circle once more, not to erase it, but to make it more visible. By holding the pencil steady, I could make the paper seem to move with me.

I lifted the brush and let it sit on the easel. The studio had changed around me. I had been painting with the same brush for a long time, but now I was watching the marks slowly settle. I did not want to cover them all. I wanted to keep them. I wanted to make sure that when I finished the painting, the paper would tell me whether it had been completed or unfinished.

I took up a small brush and touched the final edge of the sketch. There was still a faint mark there. I did not erase it. I let it remain. I was learning that the work was not finished until the marks had been acknowledged. The room around me seemed to hold its breath, too.

I returned to the paper and made one last small circle in the corner. I did not need to finish the sketch. I had already finished the idea of finishing it. I looked at the room, then at the small circle, then at the paper. Everything was still there. I had only rearranged what was already there. I was not changing the work. I was making it complete by allowing the marks to remain.

The studio was quiet. I had spent the morning in it, but the room had not given me anything new. It had simply held my attention until I asked it to do so. I put down the brush and picked up the pencil again. I began the next sketch without looking at what had already been drawn.

I did not need to finish everything on the page. I only needed to make sure that every mark would be seen.

The notebook contained a single photograph: a field of tall grass at dusk, with a single bird landing on a stalk and disappearing beneath the wind. I had spent the morning tracing the bird’s path, wondering whether it was looking for water or simply moving from one place of light to another. Its black eye was dark enough to match the soil, and when I waited for it to lift again, I found a small, silver beetle clinging to the underside of its wing.

I had never seen a beetle so perfectly matched to its host. The beetle’s shell was shaped like a miniature forest, with ridges that followed the veins of the stalk. It did not move in a straight line. It drifted, turning its head toward the sun and back again, each motion as if reading the wind.

I had been searching for a creature that moved without purpose, that chose not to be useful. A beetle is useful when it carries pollen, when it digs a tunnel, when it defends its home. But this insect seemed to be carrying nothing but the wind.

I opened the photograph again. The bird had landed and settled. The beetle had vanished into the grass, where it remained until the light changed.

The opening of the book was not about the bird or the beetle. It was about the quiet moments between them—the space where the world could be neither useful nor necessary, and where something small might begin to understand itself.
